Jack's Daily News

No. 11· 28 September 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

  1. NielsenIQ says 51% of US consumers used an AI tool to shop in the past month, and Groceryshop 2026 just spent three days teaching 4,000-plus retail executives how to hand the cart to an agent, the exact reversal of what Piggly Wiggly forced onto shoppers in 1916.

  2. Converse apologized and pulled a global Aespa Karina ad after critics said the lighting turned a skirt and a pair of dangling sneakers into KKK and lynching imagery, eight days before this issue.

  3. Fashion Week gave two opposite answers to the same problem: Marks & Spencer staged its first-ever London show to sell 57 looks at high-street prices same-day, while Prada opened an eight-floor permanent Milan flagship built around archive and art, not a single transaction.

The world

NielsenIQ · 24 Sep 2026

Majority of US shoppers now let an AI do part of the buying

NielsenIQ's new Agentic Commerce Tracker, a monthly study built on roughly 500 US consumers, found that 51% of US shoppers used at least one AI-powered tool to support a purchase in the past month, up from 42% in NIQ's own prior reading. Recommendations led the use cases at 20%, ahead of price comparison and list-building. NIQ frames this as the moment AI shopping assistance moved out of early-adopter territory and into the mainstream path to purchase.

Why it mattersThis is the first hard, repeated survey number behind a trend this brief has been tracking anecdotally since Groceryshop opened its doors on 22 September: agentic shopping is no longer a conference theme, it is a measured behavior.
The Shelby Report, Coresight Research · 22 to 24 Sep 2026, Las Vegas

Groceryshop 2026 closes with agentic commerce as the one topic everyone agreed on

More than 4,000 executives from grocery, convenience, pharmacy, dollar and club retail filled Mandalay Bay for three days built around a dedicated AI-Powered Shopping research track. Researchers from Bain, Kantar and Euromonitor presented findings on what is actually driving adoption of autonomous shopping, describing a near-future model where specialized AI agents identify a need, generate a personalized cart against a stated budget, and trigger the purchase through existing retailer systems. The Groceryshop Meetup program alone facilitated more than 30,000 business-to-business meetings on site.

Why it mattersWhen 4,000 competitors spend three days agreeing on the same bet, the bet has already been placed. The argument now is only about who captures the margin when an agent, not a person, decides what goes in the cart.
Adobe Blog, 9to5Mac · 24 Sep 2026

Adobe puts its creative tools inside Google Gemini and expands its Claude plugin

Adobe began a global rollout of Photoshop, Lightroom, Adobe Express and Firefly tools directly inside Google's Gemini assistant, live immediately across all Gemini plans, calling it "the first step" in a broader partnership with Google. On the same day, Adobe added Acrobat to its plugin for Anthropic's Claude, which now spans more than 80 tools across Acrobat, Express, Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, InDesign and Adobe Stock, rolling out globally across Claude and Claude Code.

Why it mattersThe professional creative stack is quietly becoming a layer other companies' AI assistants call into, not a destination app people open on its own, which changes who actually owns the relationship with the person making the ad.
CNN, NBC News · ad launched 27 Aug, apology 20 Sep 2026

Converse pulls a global ad and apologizes over KKK and lynching comparisons

A global Converse campaign featuring Aespa's Karina promoting the Chuck 70 X and Run Star Crush sneakers drew mounting criticism through early September: one image showed her in a white knee-length skirt lit so the fabric formed a triangular shape critics compared to a KKK hood, holding a pair of black sneakers dangling at arm's length in a way critics said evoked a lynching victim. Converse removed the ad and issued a statement: "We're sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong."

Why it mattersNobody in the production chain is reported to have flagged the composition before launch, which is the actual failure, not the intent behind a single photograph, and it is the same blind spot that keeps recurring across unrelated brands and agencies.
MediaPost, Social Media Today · 23 to 25 Sep 2026

Threads ads no longer require an Instagram identity

Meta removed the requirement that a Threads profile match an Instagram username to run ads, and businesses with no Instagram presence at all can now advertise directly from a native Threads profile. Threads-specific permissions inside Meta's business portfolio are also now independent of any linked Instagram account. Threads has reached roughly 500 million monthly active users.

Why it mattersMeta is formally admitting Threads is no longer a satellite of Instagram but a distribution channel large enough to sell on its own terms, three years after launch.

Social trends

TikTok · hot, Sep 2026

"You Probably Played With Barbie"

  • Creators overlay the line "you probably played with Barbie's growing up" on a glammed-up selfie, then cut to childhood footage of themselves button-mashing video games or wrestling with a brother, the joke riding entirely on the mismatch between polished adult and unpolished kid.
  • Creator secretlifeofdev's Mortal Kombat childhood cut pulled 422,000 likes, per Newengen's September tracking.
  • Status: hot, one of the format's clearest examples of specificity beating a generic glow-up trope.
TikTok · warm, Sep 2026

"I Try to Act Normal (and Remain Calm)"

  • Built on an audio clip ("I try to act normal, I remain calm, but this is exactly the scenario I was dreading"), the format captures painfully specific moments of external composure over internal frustration: watching someone do something the hard way when an easier option exists, a slow walker blocking a hallway.
  • No platform view count is published for the audio itself; its spread is tracked qualitatively across multiple trend blogs (Ramdam, AOL) rather than by a single verified number, flagged as such here.
  • Status: warm. This is the fourth issue in a row, after no. 8, 9 and 10, where the strongest trends reward one hyper-specific detail over a broad, relatable claim. See Content below for the first hard data behind that pattern.
Instagram Reels · early, Sep 2026

"Shared Office Pain"

  • Creators pair common workplace lines, "can we jump on a quick call?", "just circling back," with reaction clips from film and TV that show how the phrase actually lands emotionally.
  • Tracked by SocialBee's Instagram trend roundup dated 23 September 2026 as part of a wider wave of raw, relatable office content.
  • Status: early, forming alongside last issue's "Corporate Girl" without repeating it.

Campaigns & brand moves

WWD, RetailBoss, M&S Newsroom · 18 Sep 2026, London

Marks & Spencer stages its first-ever fashion show to sell same-day, not to impress

M&S marked 100 years in clothing with its debut London Fashion Week show at the Design Museum, a "see now, buy now" format modeled by Erin O'Connor, Lara Stone, Jodie Kidd and Karen Elson. The 57-look collection, 41 womenswear and 16 menswear, was designed entirely in-house and made available to buy immediately after the show, with half the pieces priced under £50. A source told WWD the retailer plans to make the show a recurring fixture.

Why it mattersAfter decades of staying off the fashion-week calendar, M&S used the format's prestige for the opposite of its usual purpose: not to sell aspiration, but to prove a high-street price point can share a runway with luxury and still sell out the same afternoon.
WWD, Wallpaper, Cultured Mag · 22 Sep 2026, Milan

Prada opens an eight-floor Milan flagship built to be visited, not just shopped

Prada Galleria opened inside Milan's historic Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II during Fashion Week: womenswear and menswear boutiques linked by an underground passage, the Marchesi 1824 pastry shop Prada acquired in 2014, private appointment salons, and "Pradasphere," the brand's first permanent exhibition tracing its history and its dialogues with art and architecture. The building hosted Vogue World 2026 for its opening.

Why it mattersPrada is betting that the highest-margin experience it can sell isn't a product at all, it's an afternoon inside the brand's own museum, with a till at the exit rather than the entrance.
Digital-News.it, Key4Biz · debuted 23 Sep 2026, Italy

Sky Mobile makes its new testimonial move in with the old one

Luca Argentero joins the long-running "Sky condominium" universe as its newest resident, welcomed by returning face Alessandro Del Piero, with the spot built entirely around the word "unlimited": Argentero's phone floods with building group-chat notifications, Del Piero raves about "unlimited friends," a neighbor hands over an envelope of "unlimited attentions." It runs across Sky's own channels, free-to-air partners TV8, Cielo and Sky TG24, plus digital, social and retail.

Why it mattersInstead of introducing a new testimonial cold, Sky spent its existing character's credibility to vouch for the new one inside a fictional world audiences already trust, a soft handover instead of a hard relaunch.

What is working in content

Hootsuite Social Trends 2026, survey of 6,500-plus marketers

Generic content strategies are now measurably losing

Hootsuite's 2026 research finds platforms have shifted from "rabbit-hole" mechanics, where one algorithm chases one click, to "snowball" mechanics, where repeated exposure to the same specific theme across many creators compounds passively. The report's conclusion: follower count is becoming an unreliable predictor of reach, and brands succeed by building deep intelligence on what a specific audience dwells on, not by running the same message across every platform. Separately, the report finds 79% of social media managers now use AI daily, but names authenticity, not output volume, as the actual differentiator between accounts that grow and those that don't.

Why it mattersThis is the first survey-level confirmation, rather than a single agency's read of one week, of the specificity-over-vagueness pattern this brief has flagged three issues running. No. 11 is not repeating an observation, it is closing it.
Socialinsider 2026 Social Media Benchmarks

Platforms reward short-form video at very different rates

Socialinsider's 2026 benchmarking data puts TikTok's average per-post engagement rate at 5.3%, against 1.8% on Instagram, 1.2% on LinkedIn and 0.9% on Facebook, with short-form video outperforming static image posts by 3.1x in interactions across the platforms studied.

Why it mattersThe same piece of short-form content earns roughly three times the interaction of a static post regardless of platform, which means the format decision now matters more than which platform gets the post first.

The historical bridge

Memphis, Tennessee · 6 September 1916

Piggly Wiggly removes the clerk. A century later, retail adds one back.

Before Clarence Saunders, buying groceries meant standing at a counter and telling a clerk what you wanted, who then fetched it from behind the counter or ladled it out of a barrel, a slow, labor-heavy process with no room for browsing. Saunders' solution, patented and opened as the first Piggly Wiggly at 79 Jefferson Street, was to remove the clerk from the transaction entirely: shoppers walked aisles themselves, picked items off open shelves, carried a basket, and paid at a fixed checkout stand, an invention still standing in every supermarket today. The idea spread so fast that by 1922 there were 1,200 Piggly Wiggly stores, briefly the largest grocery chain in the United States. Saunders had correctly identified that the clerk, meant to serve the customer, had become the bottleneck standing between the customer and the product.

Why it still holds. Groceryshop 2026 and NielsenIQ's numbers describe the exact opposite move: adding an AI agent back between the shopper and the product, deciding what to buy so the person does not have to browse at all. Saunders removed a human intermediary to speed up choice. A century later, retailers are adding a software intermediary to remove the need to choose. Both moves were sold on the same promise, that shopping should take less human effort, and both required shoppers to trust something new standing between them and the shelf.
